The paper studies four types of surface integral equation formulations: T, N, CFIE, and Müller.
The generalized minimal residual (GMRES) method is used for iterative solution of matrix equations.
Both Rao-Wilton-Glisson (RWG) and Trintinalia-Ling (TL) basis functions are used for expanding unknown surface current densities.
TL basis functions are required in N formulations to maintain solution accuracy for surfaces with sharp edges.
The choice of basis functions significantly affects the accuracy of the solution, especially for nonsmooth objects.
The Galerkin method ensures that the resulting system matrix is well-conditioned and diagonally dominant.
T formulations have symmetric matrix blocks and lower computational cost per iteration.
N formulations have nonsymmetric matrix blocks and higher computational cost per iteration.
CFIE combines equations from both T and N formulations, leading to better conditioning and improved convergence rates.
The Müller formulation is used for dielectric objects and generally leads to faster converging iterative solutions compared to the PMCHWT formulation.
The accuracy of the Müller formulation decreases compared to the PMCHWT formulation when the permittivity of the object is increased.
For composite metallic and dielectric objects, the formulations are generalized to handle multiple regions with different electromagnetic parameters.
Special care is taken at junctions where multiple regions meet to ensure accurate solutions.
The mapping properties of integral operators ensure that the basis and testing functions span the same physical spaces.
Appropriate choice of coupling coefficients can significantly improve the convergence rates of iterative solvers.
The main challenges in solving electromagnetic scattering problems with iterative methods include the conditioning of the system matrix, the choice of basis functions, and the computational cost.
The paper demonstrates that the choice of formulation and basis functions significantly impacts the conditioning of the system matrix and the efficiency of iterative solvers.
The T formulations have an additional benefit of decreased singularity of the hypersingular integral operator DDDD.
The N formulations require moving the gradient of the DDDD operator into a testing function, resulting in a line integral over the boundaries of the support of the testing function.
The JMCFIE formulation includes both T and N matrix elements, leading to higher computational cost per iteration.
The paper provides numerical examples that demonstrate clear improvements in convergence rates with the developed new formulations.
The study shows that the developed formulations lead to clear improvements in the conditioning of the system matrices and in the convergence rates when solved iteratively.
The paper highlights the importance of choosing the right formulation and basis functions for accurate and efficient solutions.
The formulations are applicable to both dielectric and composite metallic-dielectric objects.
The paper discusses the impact of internal resonances and how the developed formulations help mitigate this issue.
